The record:
Write the overview of the executive synopsis for the incident on io-shop below: a short paragraph in plain words, for the people who lead the company rather than the engineers who responded - what happened, how long it lasted, what it cost the business and the people who responded, and how it was resolved.

What a reader saw: Requests to the shop slowed down
Why, in plain words: The shop's server likely kept a note of every shopper who visited and never threw any of those notes away, so it used more and more memory the longer it ran.

Figures:
- How long it lasted: 40m 53s {duration}
- Requests failing at the worst minute: 4.0% {peak_error_rate}
- What it cost the shop in takings (estimated by Argus): none {customer_loss}
- Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one.

What was done to end it:
- Argus: restarted io-shop - confirmed
- Argus: proposed a fix, PR #531 - opened as a draft

Name {duration} and {customer_loss} in your overview.
Write no figure yourself - not in digits, not spelled out, and not as a word that sizes it ("a brief outage", "a minor loss", "tripled"). Where a figure goes, write its name, braces and all, and the synopsis writes the figure in.
Say nothing about how the incident was resolved beyond what the list of what was done says: a draft fix has not run, and nothing it would do has happened.
Speak of Argus by name, never as "we", "our" or "us": Argus is the system that responded, and each line of what was done says who did it.
Where you say who was affected, say which ones, as the cause does, or that some were, where it does not say which - never how many, and never all of them, where the cause does not say all.
Keep "likely" on what the cause says is likely, and only there.

Call submit_executive_overview with your overview.

The postmortem it is written from:
Requests to the shop slowed down
Incident: HighMemoryUsage on io-shop
Date: Nov 11, 2026, 01:44 to 02:24:53 UTC
Status: Draft. 1 of 6 action items are done.
Written by: Argus Postmortem agent, Nov 11, 2026, 02:42:06 UTC. Not reviewed yet. Each part is as of when the work it reports ended, which the timeline dates; who ended the incident is as of now.
First told: Argus posted in Slack, Nov 11, 2026, 02:24:15 UTC
Ended by: Argus: restarted io-shop - confirmed, nothing to put back

Summary
The service broke at 01:44 UTC and was back to normal at 02:24:53 UTC, 40 minutes 53 seconds later. Requests took longer: the median request went from 44.9 ms before it began to 291 ms at its worst, the slowest one request in twenty from 216 ms to 1442 ms, and the slowest one request in a hundred from 381 ms to 2490 ms. What its alert watches went from 21.6% before it began to 83.7% at its worst. The shop's takings fell short of the same hours on earlier weeks by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all. The shop's server likely kept a note of every shopper who visited and never threw any of those notes away, so it used more and more memory the longer it ran. What Argus did: restarted io-shop - confirmed, nothing to put back. Argus opened a draft fix, PR #531, for a person to review and merge. As new shoppers visit, memory in the restarted io-shop could climb toward its limit again and slow requests the way it did here.

Impact
40m 53s - onset until back to normal
4.0% - peak error rate
570 - requests failed
44.9 ms to 119 ms - p50 latency, before onset and while broken on average (worst minute 291 ms)
216 ms to 571 ms - p95 latency, before onset and while broken on average (worst minute 1442 ms)
381 ms to 1015 ms - p99 latency, before onset and while broken on average (worst minute 2490 ms)
21.6% to 55.6% - what the alert watches, before onset and while broken on average (worst minute 83.7%; the rule's line is 60%)
none - customer loss (estimated)

Root cause and contributing factors
In src/io_shop/visits.py, `record_visit`, which serve_account_page calls for each account page it serves, adds an entry for every new shopper id to the module-level dict `_LAST_SEEN`, and nothing in the files Code-Fix read removes entries except `forget_every_visit`. A long-running io-shop process therefore keeps growing in memory as new shoppers arrive, even when request volume stays flat. It rests on F1, a reading of the source nothing ran, so it is unverified.
Causal chain
symptom Requests to io-shop took longer to answer from the onset onward, at the median and even more for the slowest requests.
  Evidence:
    T4 02:24:40 Investigator Agent: Read back 361 minutes of metrics
    T5 02:24:41 Investigator Agent: Placed the start of the incident at 01:44
why 1 The io-shop process's memory kept climbing toward its container limit while requests slowed. The application logged a rising heap against its limit, and the growth was confined to the running process: the restart cleared it.
  Evidence:
    AL1 Memory usage climbing against the container limit for 15m
    G9c6f WARN io-shop: heap at #MiB of 2048MiB limit - 5 occurrences in 5 minutes, 02:00–02:04; # was 1033MiB to 1153MiB, typically 1093MiB, highest at 02:04
    M1 02:24:53 Restarted io-shop for C1: confirmed, nothing to put back
    T18 02:26:15 Mitigation Agent: Looked at the service - no longer at the incident's level since 02:24
    T19 02:26:16 Mitigation Agent: Judged the action CONFIRMED
why 2 The memory grew inside the running process with no production change to set it off. No deploy or release was found in the day before the onset, and no flag change in the hour around it. Every replica ran one revision, but the history does not name it, and the record does not show when it went out or show the service healthy after it. That revision was not ruled out.
  Evidence:
    T8 02:24:44 Investigator Agent: Read back 0 production changes
    T14 02:24:47 Argus: Read the flag provider's history - 0 flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 hour before 02:24:46
    T9 02:24:44 Investigator Agent: Read how far the deployment had rolled out - all 3 replicas run one revision, which the history does not name
  Ruled out:
    A deploy, release or flag change on the service: the Investigator Agent asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 1 day 1 minute before Nov 11 01:45; the Investigator Agent read back 0 production changes.
      T7
      T8
    A flag change by anyone but Argus: Argus read the flag provider's history - 0 flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 hour before 02:24:46.
      T14
why 3 Each account page served records the shopper in a store shared across the whole process. According to Code-Fix's reading of visits.py, that store keeps one entry for every new shopper and nothing trims it, so the process grows as new shoppers arrive.
  Evidence:
    U1 record_visit at src/io_shop/account_page.py:156, in serve_account_page: calls it: record_visit(account.shopper_id, failure)
    U2 record_visit at src/io_shop/account_page.py:160, in serve_account_page: calls it: record_visit(account.shopper_id, str(figure_cents))
    F1 What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed - nothing ran its test or its fix
Contributing factors
- Only the memory alert found the problem, and its rule waits for its condition to hold before it fires. No alert on io-shop's request latency was seen, even though latency rose from the onset. (AI-3)
- No check was seen that catches a process-wide store with no size limit before it ships. The module's own test describes the store growing without anything removing entries, and that was not flagged. (AI-4, AI-5)

Hypotheses considered
 | Hypothesis | Confidence | Result
C1 | Memory in io-shop began climbing on its own at about 01:41 UTC, from roughly 460MB to 1.8GB against a 2GiB limit, while request volume stayed at 1200. Latency rose after the heap passed about 1GiB. This is a leak in the running process: nothing was deployed or changed, and the process was never restarted. | 0.80 | confirmed
C2 | Demand saturation is a less likely alternative, because traffic did not rise. | 0.08 | never tried

Trigger
C1 was confirmed, but it names nothing specific, so no change could be matched to it.

Resolution
 | Time (UTC) | Action | By | Kind | Outcome
M1 | 02:24:53 | Restarted io-shop for C1 | Argus | nothing to put back | confirmed
 | 02:28:03 | Proposed a fix: PR #531 | Code-Fix Agent | nothing to put back | opened as a draft

Detection
The incident on io-shop began at 01:44 UTC. HighMemoryUsage fired at 02:23:52 UTC, 39 minutes 52 seconds later.
What the alert said
AL1 | Memory usage climbing against the container limit for 15m

Action items
Item | Action | Type | Owner | Tracking | Status
AI-1 | Restarted io-shop | mitigate | Argus | - | done
AI-2 | Review and merge the proposed fix | prevent | unassigned | PR #531 | open
AI-3 | Add an alert on io-shop's p95 and p99 request latency compared with its usual level, so a slowdown is caught without waiting on the memory rule. | detect | unassigned | - | open
AI-4 | Add a review or lint check to io-shop that flags module-level dicts or caches with no size bound. | prevent | unassigned | - | open
AI-5 | Audit io-shop for other module-level stores that add an entry per distinct shopper or user without ever removing any. | prevent | unassigned | - | open
AI-6 | Route HighMemoryUsage on io-shop to the on-call paging policy, so a person is paged when it fires. | process | unassigned | - | open

Lessons learned
What went well
- The alert came 16 minutes 52 seconds after its series passed its line, within the 17 minutes 30 seconds accounted for by its rule waiting 15 minutes with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute its series is read in.
- 52 seconds after the alert was raised, the Investigator Agent read back 0 production changes.
- 1 minute 1 second after the alert was raised, the Mitigation Agent restarted io-shop for C1.
- 2 minutes 24 seconds after the alert was raised, the Mitigation Agent judged the action CONFIRMED.
- 4 minutes 11 seconds after the alert was raised, the Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as a draft pull request - PR #531.
What went wrong
- The alert paged nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it.
Where it got lucky
Nothing.

Response effort
none - engineer time
142,566 - tokens spent by Argus

Supporting information
The incident's walk: http://localhost:8000/incidents/f2fbfd26-58e1-4335-bc40-146e89b233a0
The fix it proposed: PR #531 (https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/531) opened as a draft. The record holds nothing about it after that.
Changes to production read
Deploys read, none came back; flags read, none came back.
Log messages read (UTC)
Gad41 | INFO io-shop: account pages rendered normally - 5 occurrences in 28 minutes, 01:34–02:01
G46bc | ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - ClientDisconnected: the shopper closed the connection - 44 occurrences in 30 minutes, 01:35–02:04
Gbac1 | WARN io-shop: account page error rate at #% over the last minute - 26 occurrences in 30 minutes, 01:35–02:04; # was 0.50% to 4.00%, typically 1.50%, highest at 01:53
G9c6f | WARN io-shop: heap at #MiB of 2048MiB limit - 5 occurrences in 5 minutes, 02:00–02:04; # was 1033MiB to 1153MiB, typically 1093MiB, highest at 02:04
What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed - nothing ran its test or its fix
F1 | The fault is in src/io_shop/visits.py. _LAST_SEEN is a module-level dict. record_visit adds one entry for every new shopper id, and only forget_every_visit ever removes anything. The module's own docstring says Io has a few million registered shoppers and that this "holds whichever of them have been by". So a long-running process keeps growing as long as new shoppers keep arriving, even with request volume flat. That fits the incident: memory climbed with steady traffic, no deploy and no restart. tests/io_shop/test_visits.py already describes this ("nothing takes any of it away").

The fix keeps the same API but puts a cap on the store. It is now an OrderedDict holding at most _MOST_SHOPPERS_REMEMBERED (100,000) entries. record_visit writes the entry and moves it to the newest position. If the store is then over the cap, it drops the oldest entries. A shopper who comes back still costs nothing extra, and recent visitors are still remembered. Losing an entry is harmless because the module already returns None for a shopper it doesn't know, which is the normal first-visit path. Updates and evictions happen under a lock, so concurrent renders can't fight over the order. The only caller, account_page.py, imports just record_visit, and its signature is unchanged.

The new tests check two things. Recording more distinct shoppers than the cap leaves exactly the cap in memory, with the oldest gone and the newest kept. And a shopper who visits again counts as recent, so the next eviction removes someone else. Against the old code, the first test would see the count go past the cap.
How the code outside Code-Fix's patch uses what it changes, read on main
U1 | record_visit at src/io_shop/account_page.py:156, in serve_account_page: calls it: record_visit(account.shopper_id, failure)
U2 | record_visit at src/io_shop/account_page.py:160, in serve_account_page: calls it: record_visit(account.shopper_id, str(figure_cents))
Assumptions
- Exchange rate: EUR converted at 0.92191 per USD, published 2026-11-10
- No engineer minutes: no on-call incident was linked to this one, so nobody was paged to respond

✓ Impact assessed (met)
○ Root-cause analysis complete (for a person)

The document, by field:
overview: For {duration}, the io-shop online shop slowed down for some shoppers, and at the worst minute {peak_error_rate} of requests were failing. The cause was likely that the shop's server kept a note of every shopper who visited and never threw any of those notes away, so it used more and more memory the longer it ran. Argus estimates the cost to the shop in takings at {customer_loss}, and no one on call was paged to respond. To end the incident, Argus restarted io-shop, and the restart was confirmed. Argus has also proposed a fix for the underlying cause, but it is only a draft and has not been put into use yet.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {duration}, are figures code writes in from the list of figures in the ask. They are not judged.
  - The overview is written in plain words for the people who lead the company. A claim said more plainly than the postmortem says it is grounded where it means the same.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.
